# The (Lack of) Legal Framework for Geoengineering 

Thursday, September 10, 2026

 

### Susannah Dibble 

#### Staff Attorney

Sixty years ago, during the height of the Vietnam War, the United States conducted a series of covert missions over the Ho Chi Minh trail which ran from North Vietnam through Laos and Cambodia to South Vietnam. For five years, a small group of aircraft flew from bases in Thailand for weather observations. They were also carrying out a secret mission to artificially increase rainfall over the vital North Vietnamese supply lines, aiming to hamper the movement of soldiers and supplies moving south. Over thousands of sorties, U.S. Air Force planes dispersed small particles of silver iodide and lead iodide; these small particles would help form more rain droplets and hypothetically increase the rainfall over the trail.

Depending on who you asked, the impacts on the rainfall were mixed to negligible, and the biggest effect of Operation Popeye is probably the international agreement that emerged following its public disclosure. After the end of the war, the United States joined the Soviet Union and many other nations in the Environmental Modification Convention (ENMOD) which prohibits the manipulation of weather or the environment for hostile or military purposes. 

For most of the time since its adoption, ENMOD has been largely dormant, and environmental manipulation has been used only sparsely; non-military environmental modification, which the treaty explicitly says it is not designed to cover, was largely theoretical and seen as only moderately effective when deployed. This has changed as our modeling has improved with better computers, and the issue has become more urgent in the face of a warming climate. However, the legal framework has not matched pace.

As the world explores all possibilities to avert the worst impact of climate change, including geoengineering, the technology once again is moving faster than the governance and rulemaking around these controversial techniques. 

A previous blog post laid out the science and technologies of geoengineering while this post seeks to lay out existing legal frameworks and the considerations for any future framework.

### Existing International Legal Framework

There are no standalone international laws or treaties that specifically address governance of geoengineering, specifically carbon dioxide removal (CDR) and solar radiation management (SRM). While some existing instruments have tried to address aspects of geoengineering that fall within their mandate, most of these efforts have been non-binding.

The Conference of Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity has adopted decisions that give guidance to parties to not undertake any geoengineering activities that may affect biodiversity until there is adequate scientific basis and consideration of the associated risks, with exceptions for small-scale scientific research under certain conditions. The Contracting Parties to the London Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter (London Convention) and the 1996 Protocol (London Protocol) have adopted a similar resolution specific to ocean fertilization and as well as an amendment to the London Protocol that is not yet in force. The International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) Advisory Opinion on Climate Change and International Law recognized that marine geoengineering would be contrary Article 195 of the Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which outlines state obligation to prevent, reduce, and control marine pollution, if it transformed one type of pollution into another . Thus, if marine geoengineering harmed the marine environment it would be creating marine pollution in violation of Article 195. Additionally, marine geoengineering may be subject to Article 196 which outlines state obligation to prevent, reduce, and control marine pollution resulting from the use of technologies under their jurisdiction or control.

Other existing international instruments have yet to explicitly address geoengineering, either in a binding or nonbinding fashion, including the Environmental Modification Convention (does not apply to the use of techniques for peaceful purposes), the Montreal Protocol on Substances the Deplete the Ozone Layer (could apply if stratospheric aerosol injection affected the ozone layer), the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (if stratospheric aerosol injection had adverse impacts on the atmosphere, could violate air pollution standards).

### Limited Domestic Legal Framework

There are no standalone US domestic laws that specifically address governance of geoengineering. Bills have been introduced including, most recently, the Clear Skies Act (HR 4403) in 2025, which would have banned all weather modification in the United States. Three states (Florida, Louisiana, Tennessee) have passed bans on solar geoengineering and, in some cases, all forms of weather modification, including accepted practices like cloud seeding, within their states. As of July 2026, 34 other states have proposed bills to ban solar geoengineering.

Depending on the specifics of a geoengineering intervention (type, location etc.), a variety of existing federal laws (and state law equivalents) could apply. Solar geoengineering might be regulated under Title VI of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 (42 U.S.C. §7401). Marine CDR activities could be regulated under the Clean Water Act by an NPDES permit that applies the ocean discharge criteria (Clean Water Act section 403) or require an NPDES permit. Marine CDR activities could also require an MPRSA permit. If geoengineering research or activities are federally funded, taken, or permitted by federal agencies then NEPA applies and the environmental consequences must be evaluated. Research is typically excluded but there is an exception for extraordinary circumstances.

One clearly applicable federal law for all geoengineering activities is the Weather Modification Reporting Act of 1972 which requires all persons intending to engage in weather modification activities (including “modifying the solar radiation exchange of the Earth or clouds, through the release of gases, dusts, liquids or aerosols into the atmosphere”) to provide a report to NOAA 10 days prior to undertaking the activity and can be fined for failing to do so. Note that while NOAA is required by law to track weather modification activities by others, including cloud seeding, it has no authority to regulate those activities. In addition, in February 2026, GAO found that NOAA was not fully meeting its responsibilities on weather modification reporting.

### Proposed Principles for Geoengineering Research and Governance

Recognizing the dearth of comprehensive legal frameworks, different groups have proposed principles to guide geoengineering research and governance. These include the Memorandum on draft principles for the conduct of geoengineering research (Oxford Principles) (2009), Asilomar Conference Recommendations on Principles for Research into Climate Engineering Techniques (2010), The Tollgate Principles for the Governance of Geoengineering (2018), and the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Ethical Framework Principles for Climate Intervention Research (2024). These principles wrestle with similar questions around transparency, governance and oversight, public participation and consultation, consensus building, trust, accountability, justice, and responsible research.

### Implementation and Enforcement Challenges

Any future legal framework, whether domestic or international, must seek to address a variety of enforcement and implementation challenges that deployment of geoengineering technologies would entail.

Free Driver Problem – Geoengineering technology could easily be deployed by a single country or actor and yet have widespread, global effects on populations and countries who did not consent or agree to use the technology.

Moral Hazard – There are concerns that the option to address climate impacts with geoengineering technologies will lead to less commitment to address climate change impacts through mitigation and adaptation.

Long-Term Commitment – Once geoengineering technologies are used, particularly SRM, they must continue to be used so as to avoid negative impacts, such as termination shock.

Justice and Equity Concerns – Who is geoengineering benefitting? Who has the research and technology capabilities to carry out geoengineering? What would implementation of these technologies mean for intergenerational equity?

Attribution – To ensure accountability from any harms resulting from geoengineering technologies, it will be necessary to identify what counts as a harm (just direct environmental harm v. broader social/political efforts) and how to attribute that specific to a specific geoengineering use.

Public Trust and Perception – There is very little public awareness or knowledge about geoengineering, as well as few public consent activities. Local opposition has led to the cancelling of research experiments. For example, in 2021, opposition from the Sámi people in Sweden led to the cancellation of SCoPEx, an SRM experiment funded by Harvard. In 2024, the Alameda City Council voted unanimously to reject University of Washington researchers’ aerial spraying of liquefied salt from the deck of a retired aircraft carrier in San Francisco Bay after they were not notified of the project, though the researchers maintained they did not need any federal, state, or local permits.

Limited Outdoor, Site-Specific Research – The majority of ongoing research on geoengineering is limited to labs and modeling. There is a lack of outdoor, site-specific research. Thus, it is difficult to fully understand the full effects of implementing geoengineering technologies.

Delineation Between Research and Deployment – However, there are concerns about the slippery slope between research (particularly outdoor, at-scale experiments) and deployment. Questions about how to draw the line and if, on a legal level, they should be treated separately.

### Looking Ahead

As global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise and geoengineering technologies continue to develop, a comprehensive governance framework for geoengineering that prioritizes global consensus, transparency, and accountability remains a clear gap. In the absence of global agreement, domestic governments can take strides to develop their own frameworks including 1) developing principles, 2) developing a coordinated approach to federal research, 3) drafting comprehensive federal legislation, and 4) improving existing efforts to track experiments and to educate the public.
